# Affinity diagram

A workshop-style synthesis of curated customer notes into themed clusters — the same clustering discipline as sticky notes on a wall, done in minutes with the tally and vital-few themes computed for you.

Family: Voice of the customer · Format: .xlsx · Domain: core

## What it is

An affinity diagram groups a set of individually-true observations into themes — the classic version is sticky notes moved around a wall until patterns emerge. This does the same synthesis from a curated set of quotes and observations gathered ahead of time: a theme gets drafted for every note, then it's yours to reassign until the clustering feels right, with the tally updating live as you edit. Where a VOC evidence log is a running capture tool you add to over time, an affinity diagram is a discrete session on notes you've already pulled together — same underlying method, different moment in the process.

## When to use it

Use it when:

- You've already gathered a set of quotes or observations (from interviews, tickets, surveys, or gemba notes) and want to synthesize them into a small number of themes in one sitting.
- You're preparing for or running a workshop and want a first-pass clustering to react to and adjust, rather than starting from a blank wall.
- You want the vital-few themes named with a defensible tally, not just a gut sense of 'a few people mentioned pricing.'

Not when:

- You're capturing evidence as it comes in over time rather than synthesizing a curated set in one session — that's the VOC evidence log itself.
- You only have two or three notes total — there's not enough material for a clustering exercise to reveal a real pattern.
- You already know the themes and just want confirmation — genuine synthesis means letting the notes suggest the clusters, not the other way around.

## How to fill it in

- **scope** — Which accounts, segment, or population does this curated note set cover, and what prompted pulling it together for a synthesis session?
- **entries** — Enter each quote or observation you've already gathered, with its source, source type, and date. This is the curated set for the session, not everything you've ever collected.
- **themeSummary** — Drafted from your notes, then genuinely yours to edit — reassign any note's theme during the session and the clustering updates immediately, the same way moving a sticky note to a different pile would.
- **narrative** — Drafted from the top themes — what the clustering, taken together, actually suggests.
- **nextSteps** — What will the team do with this synthesis, ranked by impact and effort, owned and dated? A next step not tied to a named theme is a coaching failure mode, not a real action.

The example below is a workshop-style synthesis of nine at-risk-account notes into four themes: two tied for the largest cluster (pricing confusion and missing integrations), a third notable theme (slow support), and one single-note theme correctly left out of the vital-few list rather than forced into significance.

Full worked example, on-screen and as a downloadable .xlsx: https://www.katafacts.com/katas/affinity-diagram

## Common mistakes

- **Running the synthesis with too few notes to reveal a real pattern.** — A handful of notes can't tell the difference between a real cluster and coincidence — affinity diagramming needs enough raw material for a theme to mean something beyond one person's opinion.
- **Forcing every note into a theme, including a single outlier note that doesn't fit anywhere.** — Same vital-few discipline as every other artifact in this catalogue — a genuine one-off observation is worth noting, not stretched into a cluster it doesn't belong to.
- **Treating the first draft of theme labels as final instead of adjusting them during the session.** — The whole value of this exercise is the team reacting to and correcting the first-pass clustering together — accepting the draft without discussion skips the actual synthesis.

## What it connects to

Upstream:

- **VOC evidence log** — The curated notes an affinity-diagramming session works from typically come from an ongoing evidence log — pull the relevant subset in rather than starting from nothing.

Downstream:

- **CTQ tree** — Once a theme is named with real weight behind it, a CTQ tree is where you'd translate it into a specific, measurable requirement.

## Where AI helps

Judgement — stays with you:

- Deciding whether a drafted cluster is actually right, or moving a note to a different theme during the session
- Deciding which theme is worth acting on first

Analysis — AI helps:

- Drafting a first-pass theme label per note from its actual content
- Drafting the narrative from the top themes

Drudgery — automated:

- Tallying notes per theme and computing each theme's share of the total, with the arithmetic shown
- Identifying the vital-few top themes
- Exporting to xlsx in the house format
